title: Bouncing Golf
summary: Bouncing Golf is a mobile espionage campaign that public reporting describes as targeting users in the Middle East, with the intrusion activity delivered through trojanised Android applications rather than through desktop malware. The lures observed in reporting are themed around regional news, sport and lifestyle interests, and the applications are distributed outside official app stores, which is the detail that most distinguishes this activity from an ordinary malicious app problem: the victim must be persuaded to sideload a package, so the campaign depends on social distribution through messaging apps and links. Once installed, the malicious package presents itself as the advertised application while a background component collects device and account information, contacts, messages and files, and maintains communication with attacker-controlled infrastructure. Public analysis also describes several related modules that add capabilities such as remote command execution and location collection, and an administration layer used to manage compromised devices. Because the code lives on a phone, the evidence is rarely in enterprise network telemetry. Investigators rely instead on mobile device management inventory, application installation records from an app catalogue or sideloading history, threat intelligence feeds that list the package names and signing certificates, and logs from the messaging services used to spread the link. A common misunderstanding is that mobile malware must exploit the operating system; in this case the user grants the permissions during installation, and the malicious behaviour hides behind a legitimate-looking consent screen. Defenders should treat sideloading policy, application allowlisting and messaging-link awareness as the primary controls.

beginner.definition: Bouncing Golf is the name for a spying campaign that targets Android phones. It spreads through fake applications that look like real news or sport apps. People install them from links or chat messages, not from the official app store. Once installed, the app quietly collects information from the phone.
beginner.whyItMatters: A phone holds messages, contacts, photos, and often work email. If a spying app runs there, it can read all of that without any warning. The apps look normal on the home screen, so most people never suspect them. Company policies that block installs from unknown sources prevent this kind of attack. One careless install can expose private and work conversations.
howItWorks: The attackers build an app that looks like news, sport, or lifestyle content.
They share the app through chat messages and links, not the official store.
The victim installs it and accepts the permission requests on screen. The altered app keeps the same name and icon, so it still looks real.
The app shows its normal content, so nothing looks wrong. This is how the harmful app ends up outside the official store.
A hidden part of the app copies messages, contacts, and files. People often allow this without understanding what the permission means.
The stolen data is sent to a server the attackers control. Everything is sent quietly while the phone appears to work normally.
beginner.example: Think of a free magazine handed out at a bus stop. It looks like a real magazine, with sport results and local news. While you read it, a person beside you quietly photographs the papers in your bag. You never see them, because the magazine keeps your attention. A fake Android app works in the same way. The visible part is ordinary content, and the hidden part does the stealing while you scroll.
takeaways: Only install apps from the official store on work phones.
Check what permissions an app asks for before you accept them.
Turn on the setting that blocks installs from unknown sources.

objectives: Explain why sideloaded mobile applications are a distinct risk from official store apps.
Describe what a mobile information stealer can collect from a compromised device.
Identify the mobile management records that reveal an unauthorised application install.
Summarise how lures are distributed through messaging services rather than app stores.
Explain why operating system exploitation is not required for this campaign type.
Describe controls that reduce the chance of an unauthorised application install.
